title: Azure App Service vs Functions vs AKS
interviewQuestion: Azure App Service vs Azure Functions vs AKS — when do you use which?

story.setup: Think of three ways to feed a city: a full-service restaurant that's always open, a food-truck that shows up only when someone calls, and a whole industrial food-processing complex you operate yourself.
scenes: The restaurant (App Service) keeps its kitchen staffed and lights on all day, ready to serve a steady stream of walk-in customers at predictable cost per shift.

The food truck (Functions) drives to a location only when an order pings it, cooks that one order, and drives away — you pay only for the minutes the grill was hot, but the truck takes a moment to start its engine (cold start) if it's been idle.

The industrial complex (AKS) is a sprawling operation with many production lines (containers/pods) you personally schedule, network, and scale — total control, but you're the one running the whole facility, including the parts that never break.
A new middle-ground kiosk chain opens up (Container Apps) — containers with the food truck's pay-per-use scaling but none of the factory-management headache.

The city planner picks based on traffic pattern: steady daily crowds go to the restaurant, occasional bursts go to the food truck, and a network of many interdependent restaurants under one brand goes to the industrial complex.
story.moral: Match the compute model to the traffic shape and the ops budget — steady traffic wants App Service, bursty event-driven work wants Functions, and complex multi-service orchestration wants AKS.

analogy: App Service is a restaurant that's always open, Functions is a food truck that only fires up when called, and AKS is the factory you run yourself.
explanation: App Service is managed PaaS web hosting: you deploy a whole web app or API, it runs continuously ('Always On'), and you scale by adding instances — no cold start, low ops burden, and deployment slots give you blue-green swaps. Azure Functions is serverless and event-driven: you deploy individual functions triggered by queues, timers, blobs, or HTTP, billed per execution and memory-time, scaling automatically down to zero — the tradeoff is a cold start on the consumption plan when a function hasn't run recently. AKS is managed Kubernetes: you own container orchestration, pod autoscaling, and networking with full control, at the cost of the highest operational burden and per-node VM billing. Choose App Service for standard web apps and REST APIs with steady traffic — the default for most .NET backends. Choose Functions for event-driven, bursty work like queue processing, nightly timer jobs, blob-triggered file processing, and webhooks, where pay-per-execution makes intermittent work far cheaper. Choose AKS when you have many microservices needing orchestration, complex networking or service mesh, multi-cloud/on-prem portability, or a team with existing Kubernetes expertise — not for a single API, where the operational cost isn't justified. Container Apps sits in between: containers with serverless-style scaling and no Kubernetes management burden.
interviewAnswerShort: App Service for standard always-on web apps/APIs with steady traffic, Functions for event-driven bursty work billed per execution, and AKS for many microservices that genuinely need Kubernetes-level orchestration.
interviewAnswerDetailed: App Service is managed PaaS: you deploy a whole app, it stays warm with no cold start, scaling is instance-based, and deployment slots enable blue-green swaps — it's the default choice for most .NET web apps and REST APIs with steady traffic. Azure Functions is serverless: each function reacts to a trigger (timer, queue, blob, HTTP), scales automatically down to zero on the consumption plan, and bills per execution plus memory-time, which makes intermittent or bursty workloads — nightly reports, webhook handlers, file processing — far cheaper than keeping a whole app running; the cost is a cold start when a function wakes from idle. AKS is managed Kubernetes where you control pod scheduling, networking, and scaling yourself, billed per node/VM regardless of utilization — it earns its operational overhead only when you have many interdependent microservices, need a service mesh or complex networking, need multi-cloud/on-prem portability, or already have Kubernetes expertise on the team. I'd never reach for AKS to host a single API — that's App Service. If I want container packaging with Functions-style automatic scaling but without managing Kubernetes, Azure Container Apps is the middle ground worth mentioning.

codeExample.explanation: The Function only executes (and is billed) when a message arrives on the queue; the App Service API runs continuously and is billed per instance regardless of request volume.

mistakes: Deploying a single small API to AKS because 'Kubernetes is what serious companies use' — the ops burden isn't justified for one service.
Putting a latency-sensitive, always-hit API on the Functions consumption plan and being surprised by cold-start latency spikes.
Forgetting that App Service's 'Always On' setting must be enabled to avoid idle-timeout cold starts on the app itself.
Assuming Functions are always cheaper — for constant high-volume traffic, a Premium/Dedicated App Service plan can be cheaper than per-execution billing.
Not considering Container Apps as the middle ground before jumping straight to full AKS.

followUps.question: How do you avoid Function cold starts for latency-sensitive workloads?
followUps.answer: Use the Premium plan (pre-warmed instances) or Dedicated (App Service) plan instead of Consumption, or keep the function warm with a periodic timer ping if Premium isn't an option.

followUps.question: What are deployment slots and why do they matter for App Service?
followUps.answer: Slots are separate live environments (e.g. staging) sharing the same App Service plan; you deploy and warm up the new version in staging, then swap it into production instantly with near-zero downtime and an instant rollback path by swapping back.

followUps.question: When would you pick Container Apps over both Functions and AKS?
followUps.answer: When you want container-level control (custom runtime, any language, sidecars) with automatic scale-to-zero and traffic-splitting like Functions, but without owning Kubernetes cluster management, node pools, or networking.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Restaurant, food truck, factory — pick by traffic shape, not by hype.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a street: a lit restaurant window that never goes dark (App Service), a food truck engine that has to warm up before serving (Functions), and a factory gate you personally unlock, patrol, and lock every night (AKS).

bestPractices: Default to App Service for typical .NET web APIs unless you have a specific serverless or orchestration need.
Use Functions for anything triggered by an event rather than constant traffic — queues, timers, blob uploads, webhooks.
Reserve AKS for genuine microservice fleets that need orchestration, not for a handful of independent services.
Use deployment slots on App Service for zero-downtime releases and instant rollback.
Evaluate Container Apps before committing to full AKS if you just need containers with serverless scaling.
performanceTips: Enable 'Always On' on App Service to prevent idle unload and the resulting cold start on the next request.
Use the Functions Premium plan for pre-warmed instances when cold starts are unacceptable.
Right-size AKS node pools and use cluster/pod autoscaling instead of over-provisioning fixed capacity.

quiz.question: Which compute option scales automatically down to zero instances when idle?
quiz.explanation: Functions on the Consumption plan scale to zero and bill per execution; the tradeoff is a cold start on the next trigger.

quiz.question: Which feature of App Service enables a zero-downtime blue-green deployment?
quiz.explanation: Deployment slots let you warm up a new version in staging and swap it into production instantly, with an instant rollback path.

quiz.question: When is AKS the right choice according to standard guidance?
options: Many microservices needing orchestration and complex networking
A webhook handler that fires rarely
quiz.explanation: AKS earns its operational overhead when you have a fleet of interdependent microservices; a single API doesn't justify the ops burden.

flashcards.back: Per instance, always on — you pay whether or not requests are flowing.
Per execution plus memory-time — pay only when the function runs.
Containers, scheduled as pods, with full operator control over orchestration and networking.

flashcards.front: Middle ground between Functions and AKS
flashcards.back: Azure Container Apps — containers with serverless-style scaling, no Kubernetes management.

revision30: App Service = always-on PaaS for steady web traffic; Functions = serverless, pay-per-execution, event-driven, cold start on Consumption; AKS = full Kubernetes control for many orchestrated microservices, highest ops burden. Container Apps is the middle ground.
revision2min: App Service hosts a whole web app or API continuously, scales by adding instances, has no cold start, and gives you deployment slots for blue-green releases — it's the default for most .NET backends with steady traffic. Azure Functions deploys individual functions that react to triggers like queues, timers, and blobs, scaling automatically down to zero on the Consumption plan and billing per execution plus memory-time, which makes bursty or intermittent work much cheaper — the tradeoff is cold start latency when idle. AKS gives you managed Kubernetes with full control over pod scheduling, autoscaling, and networking, billed per node regardless of utilization; it's justified when you run many microservices that need orchestration, complex networking or a service mesh, multi-cloud portability, or when the team already has Kubernetes expertise — it's overkill for a single API. Azure Container Apps is worth mentioning as a middle ground: container packaging with Functions-like automatic scaling but without owning cluster management.
challenge: You're asked to design compute for: (1) a customer-facing REST API with steady daily traffic, (2) a job that processes uploaded images once per upload, and (3) a platform of 15 interdependent microservices with custom networking needs. Assign each to App Service, Functions, or AKS and justify each choice in one sentence.
summary: Pick compute by traffic shape and ops budget: App Service for steady always-on apps, Functions for event-driven bursty work, and AKS only when you truly need Kubernetes-level orchestration across many services.

title: Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Event Hub
interviewQuestion: Azure Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Event Hub — what's the difference and when do you use each?

story.setup: Picture a delivery company deciding how to move three very different kinds of things: sealed orders that must arrive exactly once, breaking-news alerts that everyone should hear immediately, and a firehose of sensor readings from a million trucks.
scenes: Service Bus is the registered-mail courier: each envelope (message) is a command — 'ship this order', 'charge this card' — and the courier guarantees it's delivered, keeps it in order if you ask for a queue number (session), and puts undeliverable mail in a dead-letter bin instead of losing it.

Event Grid is the town crier: the moment something happens — 'a package left the warehouse' — it shouts it to everyone subscribed, near-instantly, with no guarantee anyone was listening if their phone was off (no long retention).

Event Hub is the sensor network dashboard: a nonstop stream of readings from every truck's GPS, recorded on a rolling tape (partitioned, time-retained) that multiple analytics teams can rewind and replay independently.
The registered-mail courier never loses your payment instruction; the town crier never remembers what he shouted yesterday; the sensor tape lets you go back and replay last night's traffic pattern.
Choosing wrong means either paying enterprise-messaging overhead for a firehose of clicks, or losing an order because you used a fire-and-forget notification system for something that had to succeed.
story.moral: Match the messaging service to the job: reliable commands go to Service Bus, reactive notifications go to Event Grid, and massive replayable telemetry streams go to Event Hub.

analogy: Service Bus is registered mail that must arrive, Event Grid is a town crier shouting live news, and Event Hub is a rolling tape recorder for millions of sensor readings.
explanation: Service Bus is enterprise messaging built on queues and topics (pull model): it guarantees at-least-once delivery, supports FIFO ordering via sessions, duplicate detection, transactions, and dead-letter queues, and retains messages until they're consumed. Event Grid is a push-based pub/sub system for reactive event notifications — 'a blob was uploaded', 'a resource was created' — with high volume capacity but no ordering guarantee and only a roughly 24-hour retry window, making it lightweight and near-real-time rather than durable. Event Hub is a partitioned big-data event streaming service handling massive throughput (millions of events per second), where consumers control their own offset into the stream and multiple independent consumer groups can read and even replay the same time-retained stream. Use Service Bus when the message is a command that must not be lost — placing an order, processing a payment, dispatching a shipment — because it gives you FIFO, sessions, duplicate detection, dead-letter handling, and transactions. Use Event Grid for lightweight reactive notifications that trigger something like a Function in near real time. Use Event Hub for high-throughput telemetry ingestion — IoT devices, application logs, clickstreams, metrics — where replayability and massive scale matter more than guaranteed single delivery.
interviewAnswerShort: Service Bus is for reliable commands that must not be lost, Event Grid is for lightweight reactive notifications pushed to subscribers, and Event Hub is for massive, replayable telemetry streaming.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Service Bus models messages as commands — 'place this order', 'process this payment' — using queues and topics in a pull model, with FIFO ordering via sessions, duplicate detection, dead-letter queues for poison messages, and transactional support; it retains messages until they're actually consumed, which is exactly what you want when losing a message means losing business. Event Grid is push-based pub/sub for discrete event notifications like 'a blob was uploaded' or 'a resource was created' — it's designed for high volume and near-real-time delivery to trigger reactions like invoking a Function, but it only guarantees at-least-once delivery with a roughly 24-hour retry window and no ordering guarantee, so it's not for anything that must never be lost. Event Hub is built for ingesting massive event streams — millions of events per second from IoT devices, application telemetry, or clickstreams — using partitions for ordering-within-partition and consumer-controlled offsets, so multiple independent consumer groups can read, and even replay, the same retained stream. My one-liner: Service Bus is reliable commands, Event Grid is reactive notifications, Event Hub is massive telemetry streams — and picking the wrong one usually shows up either as lost critical messages (using Event Grid for payments) or unnecessary overhead (using Service Bus for a firehose of clickstream events).

codeExample.explanation: Service Bus sends a durable, session-ordered command; Event Grid pushes a lightweight notification to a Function trigger; Event Hub ingests one reading into a high-throughput, partitioned, replayable stream.

mistakes: Using Event Grid for financial transactions or anything that must not be lost — it lacks Service Bus's durability, ordering, and dead-letter guarantees.
Using Service Bus for high-volume telemetry (millions of events/sec) — it's not built for that throughput and adds unnecessary overhead.
Assuming Event Hub delivers exactly-once or guarantees order across the whole stream — ordering is only guaranteed within a single partition.
Forgetting to configure a dead-letter queue on Service Bus, so poison messages get retried forever or silently disappear.
Confusing 'pub/sub' as one concept — Event Grid push and Event Hub pull/partitioned streaming solve very different problems despite both being 'event' services.

followUps.question: How does Service Bus guarantee ordering?
followUps.answer: Via sessions — messages with the same SessionId are delivered in FIFO order to a single consumer processing that session, useful for per-customer or per-entity ordering guarantees.

followUps.question: What happens to an event Event Grid can't deliver?
followUps.answer: It retries with exponential backoff for up to about 24 hours (configurable), then the event is either dropped or sent to a configured dead-letter destination if one is set up.

followUps.question: Why can multiple teams read the same Event Hub stream independently?
followUps.answer: Event Hub uses consumer groups — each consumer group maintains its own offset/cursor into the partitioned stream, so one team can be at the live edge while another replays from an hour ago, without affecting each other.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Mail must arrive, news is shouted once, sensors get taped and replayed.
memoryHack.mnemonic: SB-EG-EH: Sure delivery, Grid shouts, Hub records
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a mailroom (Service Bus) with a locked ledger for every parcel, a town square with a crier shouting once (Event Grid), and a security office with a wall of rewindable CCTV tapes from a million cameras (Event Hub).

bestPractices: Use Service Bus sessions when strict per-entity ordering (e.g. per customer) is required.
Enable dead-letter queues on Service Bus so poison messages are quarantined, not lost or endlessly retried.
Design Event Grid subscribers to be idempotent since delivery is at-least-once with no ordering guarantee.
Partition Event Hub by a key (e.g. device ID) so related events land in the same partition for ordered processing.
Use consumer groups in Event Hub to let independent readers (analytics, alerting, archiving) consume the same stream without contention.
performanceTips: Batch messages when sending to Event Hub to dramatically increase throughput versus sending one event at a time.
Use Service Bus Premium tier for predictable low-latency messaging at higher, more consistent throughput.
Avoid over-partitioning Event Hub beyond your actual parallel-consumer count — more partitions than consumers wastes capacity.

quiz.question: Which service is the right choice for processing a payment that must not be lost?
options: Any of the three, they're interchangeable
quiz.explanation: Service Bus provides at-least-once delivery, FIFO sessions, duplicate detection, and dead-letter queues — exactly what a command that must not be lost requires.

quiz.question: What is the retention model of Event Hub?
quiz.explanation: Event Hub retains events for a configured time window, letting independent consumer groups replay the stream from any offset within that window.

quiz.question: Which service has no ordering guarantee at all?
quiz.explanation: Event Grid is a push-based notification system with no ordering guarantee, unlike Service Bus sessions (FIFO) or Event Hub (ordered per partition).

flashcards.back: Queues + topics, pull, at-least-once with dead-letter and transactions — for commands that must not be lost.
Push-based pub/sub for reactive, high-volume, near-real-time event notifications with a ~24h retry window.
Partitioned stream, consumer-controlled offset, massive throughput, time-based replayable retention.
Service Bus = reliable commands; Event Grid = reactive notifications; Event Hub = massive telemetry streams.

revision30: Service Bus = durable commands (queues/topics, FIFO sessions, dead-letter). Event Grid = lightweight push notifications, high volume, no ordering, short retry window. Event Hub = massive partitioned telemetry streaming with replay via consumer groups.
revision2min: Service Bus handles enterprise messaging where the message is a command that must not be lost — think placing an order or processing a payment — offering FIFO via sessions, duplicate detection, dead-letter queues, and transactional guarantees, retaining messages until consumed. Event Grid is a push-based pub/sub system for reactive notifications like 'a blob was uploaded', built for high volume and near-real-time delivery to trigger something like a Function, but with no ordering guarantee and only about a 24-hour retry window rather than durable retention. Event Hub is designed for massive-scale event streaming — millions of events per second from IoT devices, logs, or clickstreams — using partitions for ordering-within-partition and consumer-controlled offsets, so multiple independent consumer groups can read and replay the same time-retained stream. The one-liner that captures it: Service Bus is reliable commands, Event Grid is reactive notifications, Event Hub is massive telemetry streams. Picking wrong shows up as either lost critical business events or unnecessary overhead for high-volume low-stakes data.
challenge: A ride-sharing app needs: (1) reliable trip-payment processing, (2) instant notification to a Function when a driver's profile photo is uploaded to blob storage, and (3) ingesting GPS pings from 500,000 active drivers every few seconds. Assign each need to Service Bus, Event Grid, or Event Hub and justify why the other two would be wrong fits.
summary: Choose Azure messaging by the guarantee you need: Service Bus for durable commands, Event Grid for lightweight reactive notifications, and Event Hub for massive replayable telemetry streams.

title: Managing Secrets: Key Vault and Managed Identity
interviewQuestion: How do you manage secrets in Azure?

story.setup: A bank never lets a teller carry the vault key in their pocket to work every morning — instead the building itself recognizes the teller and unlocks the vault for them.
scenes: A junior developer hardcodes the database password directly into appsettings.json and commits it — the equivalent of taping the vault combination to the front door.
In development, the password moves to .NET user-secrets, stored outside the project folder — a personal notebook kept at home, never brought into the office (source control).
In production, the real password lives in Azure Key Vault — a professional vault with encryption, access logging, and rotation, far more secure than any notebook.

But now there's a new problem: how does the app authenticate to the vault without yet another secret to protect? Managed Identity solves it — Entra ID recognizes the App Service itself, like a building's badge reader recognizing an employee's face, no key needed at all.
The bootstrapping problem — 'how do I secure the credential that reads the credentials?' — dissolves, because the platform (Azure) vouches for the identity, not a stored secret.
story.moral: Managed Identity breaks the secret-securing-a-secret chain: the platform itself becomes the credential, so there's nothing left to leak.

analogy: Managed Identity is a building's badge reader that recognizes an employee's face — no physical key exists to lose or steal.
explanation: Secrets should never live in appsettings.json in source control. In development, .NET user-secrets (`dotnet user-secrets set "Db:Password" "..."`) stores values outside the project folder, keeping them off any commit. In production, Azure Key Vault is the standard: a centralized, encrypted, access-controlled, audit-logged store with built-in rotation support, wired into configuration via `AddAzureKeyVault`. The key part of the answer is Managed Identity: Azure gives the App Service or Function its own identity in Entra ID, and you grant that identity access to Key Vault, SQL, or Storage — there's no secret to store at all, because the platform handles token acquisition transparently. That solves the bootstrapping problem of securing the credential that reads the credentials. There are two flavours: system-assigned, tied to a single resource's lifecycle (created and destroyed with it), and user-assigned, a standalone identity shared across multiple resources. Also worth mentioning: App Service Configuration settings for simple non-secret config, Azure App Configuration for centralized settings with feature flags, and the discipline of never logging secret values.
interviewAnswerShort: Never in source control — use .NET user-secrets locally and Azure Key Vault in production, accessed via Managed Identity so there's no credential needed to read the credentials in the first place.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Locally, secrets go into .NET user-secrets via `dotnet user-secrets set`, which stores them outside the project folder so they can never accidentally end up in a commit. In production, Azure Key Vault is the standard store — centralized, encrypted at rest, access-controlled via RBAC or access policies, fully audit-logged, and supporting rotation — wired into the app via `builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(new Uri(vaultUri), new DefaultAzureCredential())`. The part that actually demonstrates depth is Managed Identity: Azure assigns the App Service or Function its own identity in Entra ID, and you grant that identity access to Key Vault, SQL, or Storage directly — there is no secret to bootstrap, because the platform itself handles token acquisition behind DefaultAzureCredential. That solves the classic chicken-and-egg problem: you can't store a credential to protect your credentials without needing to protect that credential too. System-assigned identity is tied to one resource's lifecycle and is simplest for a single App Service; user-assigned identity is a standalone resource you can share across multiple App Services or Functions that need the same permissions. I'd also mention Azure App Configuration for centralizing non-secret settings and feature flags separately from Key Vault, and the discipline of never writing secret values to logs or exception messages.

codeExample.explanation: DefaultAzureCredential automatically uses the App Service's Managed Identity in Azure (and falls back to local dev credentials on a developer machine), so no secret is ever hardcoded to authenticate to Key Vault.

mistakes: Committing appsettings.json with real connection strings or API keys to source control.
Storing a Key Vault access key or service principal secret in configuration instead of using Managed Identity — that just relocates the bootstrapping problem.
Using the same secret across dev, staging, and production instead of environment-scoped values.
Logging exception messages or request payloads that contain secret values.
Forgetting to grant the Managed Identity the correct access policy/RBAC role on the Key Vault, causing runtime 403s that are hard to diagnose.

followUps.question: What's the difference between system-assigned and user-assigned Managed Identity?
followUps.answer: System-assigned is created and destroyed with the resource it's attached to and can only be used by that one resource; user-assigned is a standalone Azure resource with its own lifecycle that can be attached to and shared across multiple App Services or Functions needing the same permissions.

followUps.question: How does secret rotation work with Key Vault?
followUps.answer: Key Vault supports automatic rotation policies for certain secret types, and applications using AddAzureKeyVault with a refresh interval, or the Key Vault SDK directly, can pick up rotated values without a redeploy — versioned secrets let old and new values coexist during the rotation window.

followUps.question: What's the difference between Key Vault and Azure App Configuration?
followUps.answer: Key Vault is purpose-built for secrets — encrypted, access-controlled, audited. Azure App Configuration centralizes non-secret settings and feature flags across services, and can even reference Key Vault secrets by pointer so both are managed from one place without duplicating actual secret values.

memoryHack.oneLiner: No key can be stolen if there's no key — Managed Identity is a badge, not a badge's password.
memoryHack.mnemonic: V-M-I: Vault stores it, Managed Identity fetches it, nobody carries it
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a bank vault (Key Vault) whose door opens only when it scans your face (Managed Identity) — there's no key in your pocket for a thief to steal on the subway (source control).

bestPractices: Always use Managed Identity to authenticate to Key Vault, SQL, and Storage instead of storing another credential.
Use user-secrets for local development, never real production secrets in appsettings.json.
Scope Key Vault access narrowly per identity (least privilege) using RBAC roles like Key Vault Secrets User.
Enable audit logging and alerts on Key Vault access to detect anomalous reads.
Never log or return secret values in error responses, even in non-production environments.
performanceTips: Cache Key Vault reads via configuration refresh intervals rather than calling the vault on every request.
Use user-assigned Managed Identity when many resources need the same permission set, to avoid managing dozens of separate identities.
Batch related settings into Azure App Configuration to reduce the number of round-trips at startup.

quiz.question: What problem does Managed Identity solve?
options: It removes the need to store a credential to authenticate to Key Vault
quiz.explanation: Managed Identity lets Azure vouch for the App Service's identity in Entra ID directly, eliminating the bootstrapping problem of needing a stored credential to fetch other credentials.

quiz.question: Where should local development secrets be stored?
options: Environment variables set in production only
.NET user-secrets, stored outside the project folder
quiz.explanation: .NET user-secrets keeps development-only secret values outside the repository so they can never be committed.

quiz.question: What's the difference between system-assigned and user-assigned Managed Identity?
options: System-assigned is tied to one resource's lifecycle; user-assigned is standalone and shareable
quiz.explanation: System-assigned identities live and die with their resource; user-assigned identities are independent resources that can be attached to multiple App Services or Functions.

flashcards.back: Azure Key Vault — encrypted, access-controlled, audit-logged, with rotation support.

flashcards.front: Where do local dev secrets live?
flashcards.back: .NET user-secrets, stored outside the project folder, never committed.

flashcards.front: What removes the need for a Key Vault credential?
flashcards.back: Managed Identity — Azure gives the resource an Entra ID identity and handles token acquisition.
System-assigned: tied to one resource's lifecycle. User-assigned: standalone, shareable across resources.

revision30: Never put secrets in source control. Use user-secrets locally, Azure Key Vault in production. Authenticate to Key Vault with Managed Identity so there's no bootstrapping secret at all — Azure vouches for the app's identity directly.
revision2min: Secrets should never appear in appsettings.json in source control. Locally, .NET user-secrets stores them outside the project folder via `dotnet user-secrets set`. In production, Azure Key Vault is the standard: centralized, encrypted, access-controlled, audit-logged, with rotation support, wired in through `AddAzureKeyVault`. The key insight interviewers want to hear is Managed Identity — Azure gives the App Service or Function its own identity in Entra ID, and you grant that identity direct access to Key Vault, SQL, or Storage, so there's no secret at all to bootstrap; the platform handles token acquisition transparently via DefaultAzureCredential. This solves the classic problem of how to secure the credential that reads the credentials. System-assigned identity is tied to a single resource's lifecycle; user-assigned identity is a standalone, shareable identity across multiple resources. Round out the answer with Azure App Configuration for centralized non-secret settings and feature flags, and the discipline of never logging secret values.
challenge: Your App Service needs to read a database connection string from Key Vault and also needs Storage Blob access for file uploads. Design the identity and access setup end-to-end — which identity type would you use, what permissions would you grant, and what code change is needed versus a solution using stored service principal credentials?
summary: Keep secrets out of source control entirely — user-secrets locally, Key Vault in production, accessed via Managed Identity so there's no credential left to leak.

title: Azure API Management — The API Gateway
interviewQuestion: What is Azure API Management and why use it?

story.setup: Imagine an airport with fifty different airlines each running their own separate check-in counters, security lines, and boarding gates scattered across the city — chaos for travelers and a security nightmare.
scenes: APIM builds one central terminal: every traveler (client request) walks through the same front door, no matter which airline (backend service) they're actually flying with — a single entry point that hides which gate the plane is really at.
Security screening happens once, at the terminal entrance — JWT validation, subscription keys, IP filtering — instead of every airline running its own separate metal detector.
A velvet-rope crowd-control system (rate limiting and quotas) stops any one gate from being mobbed and taking down the whole terminal.
A help desk at the terminal (developer portal) hands out maps and boarding passes (API keys, docs) so new travelers can self-serve instead of calling every airline directly.
When an airline swaps which runway it actually uses (a backend service moves or is rewritten), travelers never notice — they still walk through the same terminal gate they always did.
story.moral: APIM is the single, secured front door that decouples what clients see from how backends are actually implemented, letting services evolve underneath without breaking consumers.

analogy: APIM is a single airport terminal in front of many airlines — one security check, one entrance, regardless of which backend gate you're actually flying from.
explanation: Azure API Management is a managed API gateway that sits in front of backend APIs. It provides a single entry point — clients hit one stable endpoint while APIM routes to the right backend, so services can be moved, renamed, or rewritten without breaking consumers. It centralizes security — JWT validation, subscription keys, IP filtering, mTLS — instead of duplicating that logic in every service. It enforces rate limiting and quotas per client or subscription to protect backends from abuse, and applies policy transformations in XML (rewriting headers, converting XML to JSON, mocking responses, injecting CORS) with no backend code changes. It caches responses at the gateway to reduce backend load, offers an auto-generated developer portal for documentation and self-service key signup, and provides analytics on usage, latency, and errors per API and per consumer. It also supports versioning and revisions, letting v1 and v2 run side by side during a controlled migration. Typical use cases are exposing internal microservices to external partners, monetizing an API, or enforcing a consistent security and throttling policy across many teams.
interviewAnswerShort: APIM is a managed API gateway that gives clients one stable entry point, centralizes security and rate limiting, and lets backend services change underneath without breaking consumers.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Azure API Management sits between clients and your actual backend APIs, acting as a single entry point — consumers call one stable APIM endpoint, and APIM routes internally to whichever service actually handles it, so backends can be refactored, renamed, or replatformed without any consumer-facing break. It offloads security concerns that would otherwise be duplicated in every microservice: JWT validation, subscription key checks, IP allow-listing, and mTLS are all enforced centrally at the gateway. It protects backends with per-client or per-subscription rate limiting and quotas, so one abusive or buggy consumer can't take down shared infrastructure. Policies, written in XML, let you transform requests and responses without touching backend code — rewrite headers, convert XML to JSON, inject CORS headers, or even mock a response for a service that isn't built yet. Response caching at the gateway reduces load on the backend for repeat calls, and the built-in developer portal auto-generates API documentation and lets external consumers self-serve subscription keys instead of filing tickets. Built-in analytics show usage, latency, and error rates per API and per consumer, which is invaluable for both operations and monetization decisions. Finally, versioning and revisions let you run v1 and v2 of an API side by side and migrate consumers on a controlled timeline. I'd reach for APIM specifically when exposing internal services to external partners, monetizing an API, or needing one consistent security and throttling policy enforced across many teams' services.

    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401">

      <audiences>

    </validate-jwt>
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60"
        counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />
    <set-backend-service base-url="https://orders-service-v2.internal.azurewebsites.net" />
  </inbound>
  <backend><base /></backend>
  <outbound><base /></outbound>
</policies>

Exposing raw backend service URLs to external consumers instead of a stable APIM endpoint, coupling clients to internal implementation details.
Skipping the developer portal and manually distributing API keys and docs via email or tickets.
Not versioning APIs through APIM, forcing a breaking change onto every consumer simultaneously instead of a controlled migration.

title: Git Branching — Merge vs Rebase
interviewQuestion: How do you work with Git — branching strategy, and merge vs rebase?

story.setup: Picture two ways of writing a shared history book: one keeps every draft and correction visibly stapled in with sticky notes (merge), the other quietly rewrites your chapter as if you'd written it perfectly the first time before handing it in (rebase).
scenes: You start a new chapter on your own desk — `git checkout -b feature/order-api` — free to draft, scribble, and commit without disturbing the shared book.
Before you staple your chapter into the shared book, you tidy your own drafts into a clean, linear narrative — `git rebase` — nobody but you sees the messy first attempts.

When it's time to actually add your chapter to the shared book that others are also editing, you staple it in with a visible seam — `git merge` — so the book's history honestly shows two people worked in parallel and where they rejoined.

The golden rule of the writers' room: never silently rewrite a page that's already been photocopied and handed to other writers (never rebase a shared/pushed branch) — someone will have last week's photocopy and your rewrite will collide catastrophically.
When a page turns out to be wrong after publishing, the safe fix is to add a correction page (`git revert`), not to tear the wrong page out of everyone's copy (`git reset --hard` on shared history).
story.moral: Rebase is for tidying a story only you can see; merge is for honestly combining stories that other people already have copies of.

analogy: Rebase is rewriting your own rough draft before publishing it; merge is stapling two authors' finished chapters together with the seam left visible.
explanation: A typical branching strategy uses main (production, tagged releases), develop (integration), and short-lived feature/*, release/*, hotfix/* branches — or trunk-based development with very short-lived branches guarded by feature flags. `git merge` preserves full history and creates a merge commit, and is safe to run on shared branches because it never rewrites commits others already have. `git rebase` replays your commits on top of another branch, producing linear, rewritten history — powerful for cleaning up your own local branch before opening a PR, but dangerous on a branch that's already been pushed and pulled by others, since it rewrites commit SHAs and breaks everyone else's history. The golden rule: rebase your local work, merge shared branches. Other essential commands: `git stash`/`git stash pop` to shelve unfinished work, `git cherry-pick <sha>` to apply a specific commit elsewhere, `git revert` (a safe undo that creates a new opposite commit, safe on shared history) versus `git reset --hard` (rewrites history, dangerous if already shared), and `git log --oneline --graph` to visualize branch topology. Conflicts are resolved by editing between the `<<<<<<<` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>` markers, then `git add` and continuing the merge/rebase. Prevention is mostly discipline: pull often, keep branches short-lived, and keep PRs small.
interviewAnswerShort: Merge preserves history and is safe on shared branches; rebase rewrites history into a linear form and should only be used on your own local, unpushed commits — never on a branch others have already pulled.
interviewAnswerDetailed: My branching model is typically main for production with tagged releases, develop for integration, and short-lived feature/release/hotfix branches — or trunk-based with very short-lived branches and feature flags if the team prefers that. `git merge` combines two branches while preserving the full commit history and adding a merge commit, and it's always safe on shared branches because it never rewrites existing commits. `git rebase` replays your commits onto a new base, producing clean, linear history, but it rewrites SHAs — so I only rebase my own local branch to tidy it up before opening a PR, never a branch that's already been pushed and pulled by teammates, since that breaks their local history and causes painful duplicate-commit conflicts. That's the golden rule: rebase local work, merge shared work. Beyond that I use `git stash`/`pop` to shelve in-progress changes, `git cherry-pick` to port a specific fix to another branch, and I distinguish `git revert`, which creates a new commit undoing a change and is safe on shared history, from `git reset --hard`, which rewrites history and is dangerous once pushed. For conflicts, I resolve inline between the conflict markers, `git add` the resolved file, and continue the operation — and the best prevention is pulling frequently, keeping branches short-lived, and keeping PRs small so conflicts are rare and easy to reason about when they happen.

codeExample.code:
# Start a feature branch, commit locally
git checkout -b feature/order-api
git add . && git commit -m "Add order endpoint"

# Keep it current with the integration branch (rebase LOCAL, not-yet-pushed work)
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/develop

# Push and raise a PR — from here on, treat history as shared, never rebase again
git push origin feature/order-api

# Safe undo of an already-shared commit
git revert <bad-commit-sha>

# Resolving a conflict
# 1. open the file, edit between <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>>
# 2. git add <file>
# 3. git rebase --continue   (or git merge --continue)
codeExample.explanation: Local rebase keeps the feature branch history clean before it's shared; once pushed, further updates use merge or revert, never a destructive rewrite.

mistakes: Running `git rebase` on a branch that's already been pushed and pulled by teammates, forcing everyone into confusing duplicate-commit conflicts.
Using `git reset --hard` on a shared branch instead of `git revert`, silently discarding commits others may already have.
Force-pushing (`git push --force`) to main or develop without team awareness, overwriting others' work.
Letting feature branches live for weeks, causing painful, large merge conflicts instead of small frequent ones.
Resolving a conflict by blindly picking 'theirs' or 'ours' without reading both sides, silently reintroducing a bug.

followUps.question: When is it acceptable to force-push?
followUps.answer: Only to your own feature branch that no one else has pulled from, typically after an interactive rebase to clean up local commits — with `--force-with-lease` preferred over plain `--force` since it fails safely if someone else pushed to the branch in the meantime.

followUps.question: What's the difference between git revert and git reset?
followUps.answer: git revert creates a new commit that undoes the changes of a previous commit, preserving history and safe on shared branches; git reset moves the branch pointer (and optionally the working directory with --hard) backward, rewriting history, which is dangerous once those commits are shared.

followUps.question: What is trunk-based development and why do some teams prefer it over long-lived feature branches?
followUps.answer: Trunk-based development keeps everyone committing frequently to a single main branch (or very short-lived branches merged within a day), relying on feature flags to hide incomplete work — it minimizes merge conflicts and integration pain compared to long-lived feature branches that drift far from main.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Rebase your own draft, merge everyone else's finished pages.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture your desk (local branch) where you can shred and rewrite drafts freely, versus the shared library shelf (pushed branch) where books are already checked out by others — you never rewrite a book someone's already reading.

bestPractices: Rebase only local, unpushed commits; merge (or PR) once a branch is shared with others.
Keep feature branches short-lived and PRs small to minimize conflict surface area.
Use `git revert` for undoing changes on shared branches instead of history-rewriting resets.
Pull/fetch frequently to catch conflicts early while they're small and easy to resolve.
Use `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force` when force-pushing your own branch, to avoid silently overwriting a teammate's push.
performanceTips: Use `git log --oneline --graph --all` to quickly visualize branch topology before deciding merge vs rebase.
Squash noisy local commits via interactive rebase before opening a PR, so reviewers see one coherent change.
Use shallow clones or sparse checkouts in CI pipelines for large repos to speed up pipeline checkout time.

The golden rule is rebase your local work, merge shared branches. Other essentials: git stash/pop to shelve in-progress work, git cherry-pick to port a specific commit elsewhere, and git revert (safe, creates an undo commit) versus git reset --hard (rewrites history, dangerous once shared). Conflicts are resolved by editing between the conflict markers, staging the resolved file, and continuing the operation — prevented in the first place by pulling often, using short-lived branches, and keeping PRs small.

title: CI/CD with Azure DevOps
interviewQuestion: How do you implement CI/CD with Azure DevOps?

story.setup: Think of a relay race with a strict rulebook: every runner (developer) must pass the baton (code) through a series of checkpoints before it's allowed anywhere near the finish line (production).
scenes: Continuous Integration is checkpoint one: the moment a runner hands off the baton — every push — an official immediately verifies it's the real baton (build succeeds) and hasn't been tampered with (tests pass), catching problems in minutes, not weeks.

The baton then travels through a gauntlet of increasingly serious checkpoints — Dev auto-clears it, QA auto-clears it, but Staging and Production have a human official standing guard who must wave it through (approval gates) before it proceeds.

At the Production checkpoint, the race organizers install a second, parallel track right next to the finish line (a deployment slot) — the new baton warms up there first, and the swap to 'official' happens instantly, so if it stumbles, they can swap it right back with zero downtime.
Every checkpoint pulls its secret keys — passwords, connection strings — from a guarded vault (Key Vault) rather than carrying them pinned to the runner's jersey (hardcoded in config).
Off to the side, a scoreboard (Azure Boards) tracks which sprint each baton-carrying feature belongs to, while the whole race is recorded step by step (Pipelines) for anyone to audit later.
story.moral: CI catches problems within minutes of every push; CD turns a validated build into a series of gated, reversible steps toward production, never a single risky leap.

analogy: CI/CD is a relay race with checkpoints — every handoff is verified immediately, and only a human-approved baton gets anywhere near the production finish line.
explanation: Continuous Integration means every push triggers an automated build and test run, so integration problems surface within minutes rather than being discovered weeks later at merge time. Continuous Deployment/Delivery means a validated build flows automatically through a chain of environments, with manual approval gates protecting the more sensitive ones. A typical Azure Pipelines YAML build stage restores dependencies, builds in Release configuration, runs tests while collecting code coverage, publishes the app, and publishes build artifacts for the release stage to consume. The release pipeline then promotes that same artifact through Dev (auto-deployed), QA (auto-deployed), Staging (requires approval), and Production (requires approval), with environment-specific variables and secrets pulled from Key Vault rather than hardcoded per stage. Deployment slots on App Service enable zero-downtime swaps and near-instant rollback by warming up the new version in a staging slot before swapping it into production. Azure DevOps as a platform is made up of Boards (work items, sprints), Repos (git hosting), Pipelines (build/release automation), Artifacts (package feeds), and Test Plans (manual/exploratory testing). When describing your own experience honestly, it's fine to say you worked within existing pipelines — ensuring your PR built cleanly, tests passed, and coverage gates held — and triggered or debugged releases, without necessarily having authored pipelines from scratch; that's credible and specific.
interviewAnswerShort: CI runs build and tests automatically on every push to catch problems fast; CD promotes that validated build through Dev, QA, Staging, and Production with approval gates and deployment slots for zero-downtime, reversible releases.
interviewAnswerDetailed: Continuous Integration means every push to develop or main triggers an automated pipeline that restores, builds, and runs tests — typically with code coverage collected via `--collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"` — so integration issues are caught within minutes instead of at a painful merge weeks later. Continuous Deployment takes that same validated build artifact and promotes it through a chain of environments: Dev and QA usually auto-deploy since the risk is low, while Staging and Production sit behind manual approval gates, with each environment having its own variables and secrets sourced from Key Vault rather than duplicated per stage. On App Service, deployment slots let you warm up the new version in a staging slot and then swap it into production instantly, which gives you both zero-downtime releases and an instant rollback path if something's wrong — you just swap back. Azure DevOps as a suite covers Boards for work items and sprint tracking, Repos for git hosting, Pipelines for the actual build/release automation, Artifacts for package feeds, and Test Plans for manual and exploratory testing. In an interview I'd be precise about my actual experience level: if I've worked within existing pipelines — making sure my PR builds cleanly, tests pass, and the coverage gate holds before merge, and I've triggered QA releases and debugged failed builds — I'd say exactly that rather than overclaiming that I've authored pipelines from scratch, because specific and honest answers land better than vague confident ones.

trigger:
  branches:
    include: [develop, main]

pool:
  vmImage: 'windows-latest'

steps:
  - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
    inputs: { command: 'restore' }

  - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
    inputs: { command: 'build', arguments: '--configuration Release' }

  - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2

Hardcoding environment-specific secrets in pipeline YAML instead of pulling them from Key Vault per environment.
Deploying straight to production with no staging slot or approval gate, turning every release into an all-or-nothing risk.

Letting a broken pipeline stay red for days, training the team to ignore failed build notifications.

followUps.question: How do deployment slots enable zero-downtime deployment and instant rollback?
followUps.answer: The new version is deployed and warmed up in a separate staging slot with its own URL while production keeps serving traffic; a swap operation exchanges the slots' routing (and optionally settings) atomically, so users see the new version instantly with no downtime, and if there's a problem you swap back just as fast for an instant rollback.

followUps.question: What's the difference between a build (CI) pipeline and a release (CD) pipeline in Azure DevOps?
followUps.answer: The build pipeline compiles, tests, and packages the code into an artifact on every push — it's about validating the code. The release pipeline takes that already-validated artifact and deploys it through a sequence of environments with approvals, gates, and environment-specific configuration — it's about promoting and releasing, not rebuilding.

followUps.question: Why put approval gates on Staging and Production but not Dev/QA?
followUps.answer: Dev and QA are low-risk, frequently-updated environments where fast automatic feedback matters more than caution; Staging and Production carry real business or customer risk, so a human approval step ensures a person consciously signs off before code reaches customers or a production-like environment.

memoryHack.memoryPalace: Picture a relay race with an official at every handoff verifying the baton (CI), and a fenced VIP lane near the finish line where a guard must personally wave the baton through before it reaches the crowd (CD approval gate).

Collect code coverage in the test step and gate merges on it holding steady or improving.
Pull environment secrets from Key Vault per stage instead of duplicating them in pipeline variables.
Use deployment slots for zero-downtime releases with an instant rollback path.

title: Writing Unit Tests — AAA, xUnit, and Moq
interviewQuestion: How do you write unit tests?

story.setup: A chemistry teacher never tests a new reaction in the middle of a room full of other ongoing experiments — she isolates it on its own bench with only the reagents she controls.
scenes: Arrange is setting up the bench: fake reagents (mocked dependencies like INotificationService, IOrderRepository) stand in for the real, unpredictable chemicals so the experiment only tests one thing.
Act is the single reaction she triggers — calling service.PlaceOrder(order) — nothing else happens on the bench at that moment.
Assert is reading the litmus paper afterward: did the mock repository actually get told to Save, did the mock notifier actually get told to Send — Times.Once, not zero, not twice.

A student who writes `new EmailService()` directly inside the class under test has welded the reagent bottle shut — there's no way to swap in a fake, so the class can never be tested in isolation; DI and interfaces are what make the swap possible in the first place.

The teacher never grades a student for cleaning the bench (getters) or for the equipment manufacturer's engineering (framework code) — only for actual chemistry: business logic, edge cases, and what happens when the reaction goes wrong.
story.moral: A unit test isolates one class with mocked dependencies to verify one behavior fast and repeatably — dependency injection is what makes that isolation possible at all.

analogy: A unit test is a chemistry experiment run alone on its own bench with fake reagents standing in for anything you don't control.
explanation: Unit tests follow the AAA pattern — Arrange (set up the object under test and mock its dependencies), Act (call the one method being tested), Assert (verify the outcome and that dependencies were called as expected). A unit test isolates one class with all its dependencies mocked, runs fast, and never touches a real database or network; an integration test exercises real components together, often via WebApplicationFactory for ASP.NET Core APIs. Dependency injection and coding to interfaces are what make a class testable in the first place — a class that does `new EmailService()` internally has no seam for a test double, so it can never be unit tested in isolation. xUnit's [Fact] marks a single test case; [Theory] with [InlineData(...)] runs the same test body against multiple parameter sets, which is efficient for boundary and edge-case coverage. Moq lets you create a fake implementation of an interface (`new Mock<IOrderRepository>()`), configure its behavior with `.Setup(...).Returns(...)` or `.ReturnsAsync(...)` for async methods, and verify interactions afterward with `.Verify(..., Times.Once)`. What actually scores in interviews: knowing the unit-vs-integration distinction, understanding why DI enables testability, testing business logic/edge cases/error paths rather than trivial getters or framework code, and the FIRST principles — tests should be Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, and Timely.
interviewAnswerShort: I follow AAA — arrange mocked dependencies with Moq, act by calling the method under test, and assert both the return value and that the mocks were called as expected — keeping each test fast, isolated, and focused on one class's business logic.
interviewAnswerDetailed: I structure every unit test with the AAA pattern: Arrange sets up the object under test with its dependencies mocked via Moq — for example `new Mock<IOrderRepository>()` — so the test never touches a real database or network call; Act invokes the single method being tested; Assert checks both the return value with Assert.Equal/Assert.Throws and, via `mock.Verify(x => x.Save(order), Times.Once)`, that the right interactions happened with the right arguments the right number of times. The reason this is possible at all is dependency injection and coding to interfaces — a class that instantiates `new EmailService()` internally has welded itself to a concrete dependency with no seam for a test double, so DI isn't just an architecture preference, it's what makes unit testing achievable. I use xUnit's [Fact] for a single test case and [Theory] with [InlineData] to run the same assertion logic against multiple input/expected-output pairs, which is great for covering boundary values like zero, negative, and valid amounts efficiently. For async repository methods I configure Moq with `.Setup(r => r.GetByIdAsync(5)).ReturnsAsync(order)` rather than `.Returns`. I clearly separate unit tests, which isolate one class with everything mocked and run in milliseconds, from integration tests, which exercise real components together — for ASP.NET Core APIs I'd reach for WebApplicationFactory to spin up an in-memory test server. I focus test coverage on business logic, edge cases, and error paths rather than trivial getters or framework plumbing, and I keep the FIRST principles in mind — tests should be Fast, Independent of each other, Repeatable in any environment, Self-validating with a clear pass/fail, and Timely, written close to when the code is written.

title: What to Look for in a Code Review
interviewQuestion: What do you look for in a code review?

story.setup: A building inspector doesn't just check if the house looks nice — they walk through in a strict order: structural safety first, then wiring, then whether the paint matches the neighborhood.
scenes: First stop, the foundation: does it actually meet the blueprint's requirements, and does it survive the edge cases — an empty room, a doorway of zero width, a load right at the boundary (correctness, null/empty/zero/boundary checks).

Next, the wiring behind the walls: are the electrical panels locked (parameterized queries, no secrets in code), and does every door actually check the resident's key before opening (authorization checked server-side, not just a hidden door in the UI)?
Then the inspector times how fast water reaches the tap: any pipe fetching one drop at a time in a loop when a single big pipe would do (N+1 queries, SELECT *, missing async on I/O)?

They check the fire safety plan: does a small kitchen fire get silently smothered and forgotten (swallowed exceptions, throw ex resetting the stack trace), or properly reported to the fire department (rethrown with throw;, resources released via using)?

Finally, cosmetic and consistency checks: are the room labels clear (naming), is there junk left in the hallway (dead code, magic numbers), and does this house match the style of every other house on the street (team conventions) — and did anyone actually write down what happens if the smoke detector goes off (tests for failure paths)?
story.moral: A good code review walks the same priority order every time — correctness and security first, then performance, then readability — because catching a structural flaw matters infinitely more than catching a typo.

analogy: A code review is a building inspection: structural safety and wiring first, cosmetics last — never the other way around.
explanation: Correctness comes first: does the change meet the requirement, and does it handle edge cases — null, empty, zero, boundary values? Security is checked next: parameterized queries (never string-concatenated SQL), no secrets in code, input validated, and authorization checked server-side rather than assumed from a hidden UI element. Performance issues to catch: N+1 queries, SELECT * pulling unnecessary columns, missing async on I/O-bound calls, loading entire tables into memory, and string concatenation inside loops instead of StringBuilder. Error handling matters — exceptions should never be silently swallowed, `throw;` preserves the original stack trace while `throw ex;` resets it and hides the real failure point, and disposable resources belong in a `using` statement. Readability and design get checked too: clear names, one responsibility per method, no dead code, no unexplained magic numbers. Tests are part of the review — new logic needs unit tests, including failure paths, not just the happy path. Consistency with the team's existing patterns rounds it out, since a locally clever but inconsistent approach adds cognitive overhead for everyone else. The way to communicate this in an interview: correctness and security first, then performance, then readability; keep comments specific and non-personal ('this could throw if the list is empty' rather than 'this is wrong'); and clearly distinguish blocking issues from suggestions so the author knows what must change versus what's optional.
interviewAnswerShort: I check correctness and edge cases first, then security — parameterized queries, server-side authorization, no secrets — then performance issues like N+1 queries or missing async, then error handling, readability, and test coverage, roughly in that priority order.
interviewAnswerDetailed: My review priority is deliberately ordered: correctness first — does the change actually meet the requirement, and does it handle null, empty, zero, and boundary inputs — because a functionally wrong change is the most expensive kind of bug to ship. Security comes right after: I check for parameterized queries instead of string-concatenated SQL, no secrets hardcoded anywhere, input validation, and critically, that authorization is enforced server-side on every endpoint with actual resource-ownership checks like `if (order.UserId != currentUserId) return Forbid();` — hiding a button in the UI is not security. Then performance: N+1 query patterns, SELECT * pulling more than needed, missing async on I/O-bound calls, loading whole tables into memory, and string concatenation inside loops. Error handling gets specific attention too — exceptions shouldn't be silently swallowed, `throw;` should be used instead of `throw ex;` to preserve the original stack trace, and disposable resources should be wrapped in `using`. Readability and design matter but come after the substantive issues: clear naming, single-responsibility methods, no dead code or magic numbers. I also check that new logic has unit tests covering failure paths, not just the happy path, and that the change is consistent with the team's existing patterns rather than introducing a locally clever but inconsistent approach. When leaving comments, I keep them specific and non-personal — 'this could throw if the list is empty' rather than 'this is wrong' — and I clearly flag which comments are blocking versus which are just suggestions, so the author isn't left guessing what actually needs to change before merge.

mistakes: Reviewing only for style/formatting and missing actual correctness or security issues.
Trusting that a hidden or disabled UI button is sufficient authorization instead of requiring a server-side check.
Approving a PR with new business logic and no accompanying unit tests, including failure-path tests.
Leaving vague or personal comments ('this is bad code') instead of specific, actionable, non-personal feedback.
Not distinguishing blocking issues from optional suggestions, leaving the author unsure what actually has to change.

followUps.question: Why is `throw;` preferred over `throw ex;` when rethrowing?
followUps.answer: `throw;` preserves the original exception's stack trace, showing exactly where the failure first occurred; `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to the rethrow point, hiding the real origin and making production debugging much harder.

followUps.question: Why is hiding a button in the UI not sufficient authorization?
followUps.answer: A client can call the API endpoint directly regardless of what the UI shows or hides, so if the server doesn't independently verify the caller is authorized and owns the resource, hiding a button provides no real security — authorization must be enforced server-side on every request.

followUps.question: What's an N+1 query and why does a reviewer flag it?
followUps.answer: It's a pattern where a loop fetches related data one row at a time — one query to get a list, then N more queries, one per item — instead of a single batched query; it's a common performance killer that's often invisible in dev with small data but devastating at production scale.

Flag string concatenation inside loops in favor of StringBuilder for anything beyond a handful of iterations.

title: Security Best Practices in .NET
interviewQuestion: What are the security best practices you follow in .NET?

story.setup: Picture a castle under siege from eight different directions at once — a spy slipping forged orders into the mail room, a thief in the crowd, a con artist tricking a guard into opening the gate from inside.
scenes: The mail room clerk (SQL layer) is trained to never blindly paste a stranger's note into an official order — every message is checked against a fixed template (parameterized queries), so no forged command like 'DROP the treasury' can sneak through as if it were data.

The armory guards store gunpowder (passwords) properly sealed and salted so that even if the vault is breached, the powder can't be reused directly — never left as loose plain powder (plaintext/MD5/SHA1) anyone could scoop up.

A con artist plants a poisoned scroll in the town square hoping a guard reads it aloud and it starts issuing commands in the guard's voice (XSS) — the castle's scribes automatically encode anything posted publicly, and the guard's real orders (JWT) are kept in a locked box (HttpOnly cookie) the scroll-reader can never open.

Someone forges a letter that looks like it's from the king asking the gate to open, but the gate demands a wax seal only the real king's office produces (CSRF token / anti-forgery), so the forged letter alone can't move the gate.

A servant tries to overhear a room number and simply requests that the door open, and the guard checks his own list of who's actually allowed in that room instead of trusting the servant's claim (broken access control) — and no clerk ever accepts a customer's own note claiming 'I am now the treasurer' (over-posting) without validating it against the real, protected fields.
story.moral: Every layer of a .NET application faces its own specific attack shape, and each has a specific, well-known defense — the discipline is applying all of them, not just the ones that are top of mind.

analogy: Application security is a castle under siege from eight directions at once — every gate, mail room, and scroll needs its own specific defense.
explanation: SQL Injection: always parameterize — Entity Framework parameterizes automatically via LINQ, and raw ADO.NET should use `cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue`, never string-interpolated SQL. Passwords: hash with bcrypt, Argon2, or PBKDF2 with a salt — never MD5, SHA1, or plaintext, since those are either broken or unsalted-fast and trivially crackable at scale. XSS: Razor encodes output by default, so the real danger is `@Html.Raw` bypassing that encoding — and keeping JWTs in HttpOnly cookies means an injected script can't read them via document.cookie even if XSS occurs. CSRF: `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` plus SameSite cookies prevent a forged cross-site request from acting on a user's behalf. Secrets: Key Vault or user-secrets, never in source control. Broken access control: authorize server-side on every endpoint and verify actual resource ownership — `if (order.UserId != currentUserId) return Forbid();` — because hiding a UI button is not security, a client can call the API directly. Over-posting: bind to DTOs rather than entities directly, so a client can't set fields like `IsAdmin = true` that were never meant to be client-writable. Beyond these: HTTPS everywhere, rate limiting, CORS whitelisting (not wildcard-with-credentials), security headers, dependency scanning for known-vulnerable packages, and returning generic client-facing error messages while logging full detail server-side so stack traces never leak to an attacker.
interviewAnswerShort: Parameterize all SQL, hash passwords with bcrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2 plus salt, rely on Razor's default encoding and avoid @Html.Raw for XSS, use anti-forgery tokens for CSRF, keep secrets in Key Vault, enforce authorization server-side on every endpoint, and bind to DTOs instead of entities to prevent over-posting.
interviewAnswerDetailed: I treat this as a layered checklist. For SQL injection, I always parameterize — EF Core does this automatically through LINQ, and any raw ADO.NET goes through `cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue`, never string interpolation into a query. Passwords are always hashed with a slow, salted algorithm like bcrypt, Argon2, or PBKDF2 — never MD5 or SHA1, which are either cryptographically broken or fast enough to brute-force at scale without a proper work factor. For XSS, I lean on the fact that Razor encodes output by default, so the actual risk surface is `@Html.Raw` bypassing that encoding, and I keep JWTs in HttpOnly cookies specifically so that even if an XSS payload executes, it can't read the token via JavaScript. For CSRF, `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` combined with SameSite cookies stops a forged request originating from another site from acting on an authenticated user's behalf. Secrets go in Key Vault in production and user-secrets locally — never in source control. The one I emphasize most is broken access control: authorization has to be checked server-side on every endpoint, verifying actual resource ownership like `if (order.UserId != currentUserId) return Forbid();`, because hiding a button in the UI is not security — a client can call the API directly regardless of what's rendered. Over-posting is the other one I specifically watch for: binding request bodies to DTOs rather than entity classes directly, so a client can't set a field like IsAdmin that was never meant to be client-writable, just because the model happened to expose it. Rounding it out: HTTPS everywhere, rate limiting, a real CORS whitelist rather than a wildcard combined with credentials, standard security headers, scanning dependencies for known vulnerabilities, and returning generic error messages to clients while logging full exception detail only server-side.

codeExample.explanation: Each snippet defends against one specific attack: SQL injection via parameterization, weak password storage via a proper hasher, broken access control via a server-side ownership check, and over-posting via DTO binding that excludes sensitive fields.

mistakes: Building SQL with string interpolation or concatenation instead of parameterized queries or LINQ.
Hashing passwords with MD5 or SHA1, or storing them without a salt.
Using @Html.Raw on user-supplied content, reintroducing XSS that Razor would otherwise prevent by default.
Binding request bodies directly to entity classes, letting a client set fields like IsAdmin or Role that should never be client-writable.
Trusting client-side authorization (a hidden button, a disabled menu item) instead of checking ownership and permissions server-side on every request.

followUps.question: Why is bcrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2 preferred over SHA-256 for password hashing?
followUps.answer: General-purpose hashes like SHA-256 are designed to be fast, which is exactly the wrong property for password storage — it lets an attacker with a stolen hash database try billions of guesses per second. bcrypt, Argon2, and PBKDF2 are deliberately slow and configurable (work factor/iterations), and they incorporate salting, making brute-force and rainbow-table attacks impractical.

followUps.question: How does keeping a JWT in an HttpOnly cookie mitigate XSS impact?
followUps.answer: HttpOnly cookies are inaccessible to JavaScript (document.cookie can't read them), so even if an XSS payload successfully executes on the page, it cannot steal the token to impersonate the user elsewhere — it limits the blast radius of an XSS vulnerability rather than preventing XSS itself.

followUps.question: What's the difference between over-posting and broken access control?
followUps.answer: Over-posting is a client setting unintended fields on a request body (like IsAdmin) because the server bound directly to an entity exposing that field; broken access control is a server failing to verify that the authenticated user is actually allowed to act on the specific resource requested, regardless of what fields are in the request.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Every gate of the castle needs its own guard — no single lock protects them all.
memoryHack.mnemonic: SPXCSBO: SQLi, Passwords, XSS, CSRF, Secrets, Broken access control, Over-posting
memoryHack.memoryPalace: Walk the castle wall: the mail room (parameterized SQL), the armory vault (salted password hashes), the town scroll-reader (Razor encoding + HttpOnly), the gate demanding a wax seal (anti-forgery token), the treasury (Key Vault), the guard checking his own list (server-side authorization), and the clerk who ignores a customer's self-written title (DTO binding).

Hash passwords with bcrypt, Argon2, or PBKDF2 plus salt — never MD5, SHA1, or plaintext.
Bind incoming requests to DTOs, never directly to entity classes, to prevent over-posting.
Enforce authorization and resource-ownership checks server-side on every endpoint, never rely on UI-only restrictions.
Keep secrets in Key Vault/user-secrets, enforce HTTPS everywhere, and return generic client errors with full detail logged only server-side.
performanceTips: Tune bcrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2 work factor to balance security against login latency — too high slows every login, too low weakens protection.
Cache CORS and security header configuration rather than recomputing per request.
Rate-limit authentication endpoints specifically, since they're the highest-value target for brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks.
